title: Fingerprints in 15,000 year old clay show children helped make figurines at Natufian sites
dek: A re-examination of heated clay fragments from three Israeli sites reveals 154 figurative objects, pushing the region's symbolic clay tradition back into the Epipalaeolithic.
body: You can still see the fingerprints. Microscopic examination of 154 clay artefacts from el-Wad Terrace, Hayonim Terrace, and Eynan-Mallaha reveals fingertip depressions, palm impressions, and the distinct marks of shaping, smoothing, grooving, and incision left by the people who handled them 15,000 years ago.

The fragments come from the Natufian culture, hunter-fisher-gatherers who began settling down in Southwest Asia millennia before agriculture took hold. Until this study, published in PLOS One, only two clay figurines were known from the entire Natufian record. The new assemblage includes 15 complete figurines and 139 cylindrical fragments interpreted as pieces of figurative objects.

Eleven of the figurines are birds. Several show cylindrical necks and downward-facing heads, a posture researchers suggest mimics the courtship displays of waterfowl like ducks, geese, or swans. Others may depict birds of prey. The recurrence of these forms across three separate sites points to an established tradition, not isolated experiments.

Two fragments represent hoofed animals. One, possibly a mountain gazelle, bears small impressions where perishable materials, perhaps twigs, were inserted to represent horns or antlers. If correct, this is among the earliest known composite figurines in Southwest Asia, combining clay with organic elements that have long since vanished.

Human forms appear too. One fragment shows an upper body with modelled arms. Another is a stylised face that may have held decorations of grasses, fibres, hair, or feathers. Ten of the eleven bird figurines carry traces of red colouring. One Early Natufian piece was coated with an iron-rich clay slip, an engobe technique applied and possibly smoothed with a finger, with an uncoloured diagonal line left by a plant fibre stencil, the earliest known evidence for this method.

Every object was heated, though researchers cannot yet say if they were fired intentionally in a kiln-like setting, passively warmed near hearths, or accidentally burned after deposition. Further analysis will target their heating histories and the temperatures they reached. The manufacturing traces already tell a social story: fingerprints show both children and adults made these objects, revealing the demographics of craft production in communities transitioning toward sedentary life.

The findings push part of Southwest Asia’s so-called “revolution of symbols” back into Epipalaeolithic times. Developments in symbolic expression and clay technology were underway among hunter-gatherers before the Neolithic. A mature figurative tradition existed where textbooks long placed only pigments and isolated experiments.
doesnt_show: The study does not show whether the figurines served ritual, decorative, or pedagogical purposes, nor does it confirm intentional firing versus accidental burning. The composite animal interpretation relies on negative impressions where organic material decayed.
settle: Controlled refiring experiments and residue analysis on the engobe-coated figurine would clarify firing intent and pigment technology.
